# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterized by delayed opacification of the distal coronary vasculature in the absence of obstructive epicardial disease. The coronary slow flow phenomenon is an angiographic finding characterized by delayed distal vessel opacification in the absence of significant epicardial coronary disease. It was first described in 1972, when Tambe et al first described the SCF phenomenon in six patients with chest pain. [1] More than five decades later, CSFP remains incompletely understood, yet it is increasingly recognized as a clinically meaningful disorder of the coronary microcirculation. The coronary slow flow phenomenon is an important angiographic entity characterized by delayed progression of the injected contrast medium through the coronary tree. It is a frequent finding, typically observed in patients presenting with acute coronary syndromes. Although it is well known to interventional cardiologists for approximately four decades, the pathogenic mechanisms remain unclear. [2]

## Definition and Diagnosis

CSFP must be distinguished from secondary causes of impaired coronary filling. It has been accepted as an independent clinical entity, called 'CSFP', 'coronary slow flow syndrome', 'syndrome Y', or "primary" coronary slow flow. Importantly, 'primary' CSFP should be distinguished from the delay in the contrast progression in the context of coronary reperfusion therapy such as angioplasty or stenting for acute myocardial infarction, or other "secondary" causes of coronary slow flow. These include coronary artery ectasia, coronary artery spasm, valvular heart disease, or connective tissue disorders. [3]

Quantification relies on the corrected Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) frame count (CTFC), introduced by Gibson and colleagues. In normal patients and patients with acute myocardial infarction, the number of cineframes needed for dye to reach standardized distal landmarks was counted to objectively assess an index of coronary blood flow as a continuous variable. The TIMI frame-counting method was reproducible. [4] Because the left anterior descending artery (LAD) is longer, the longer LAD frame counts were corrected by dividing by 1.7 to derive the corrected TIMI frame count. [4] In practice, CSF is characterized by normal or near-normal epicardial coronary arteries (stenosis < 40%) with delayed distal vessel contrast opacification, as evidenced by either TIMI 2 flow or a corrected TIMI frame count > 27 frames in at least one epicardial vessel. [5] Guidelines have since recognized CSFP as a marker of microvascular dysfunction, although this equivalence has been questioned. Guidelines recommend that coronary slow flow phenomenon, defined as corrected TIMI frame count > 27, can diagnose coronary microvascular dysfunction in patients with angina and nonobstructed coronary arteries. CSFP has also historically been regarded as a sign of coronary endothelial dysfunction. [6]

## Epidemiology

CSFP is not rare among patients referred for angiography. It has an incidence of 1–5% in patients undergoing coronary angiography and has been most frequently found in young men who are smokers with metabolic syndrome. [7] In a large series, CSFP was identified in 96 (5.5%) subjects referred for angiography. Subjects with CSFP were more obese and had lower high-density lipoprotein levels. [8] Early case-control data established its association with smoking and acute presentations, noting that patients with coronary slow flow differed from controls, more often being current smokers and presenting with rest pain requiring urgent admission, usually to the coronary care unit. [9]

## Pathophysiology

Several overlapping mechanisms have been proposed. Small-vessel disease has been implicated since the earliest descriptions; endomyocardial biopsy studies revealed pathologic small coronary arteries with fibromuscular hyperplasia, hypertrophy of the media, myointimal proliferation, and endothelial degeneration. [10] Hemodynamic and metabolic studies support a state of heightened resting microvascular tone, demonstrating that resting coronary sinus oxygen saturation was low compared with control subjects, reflecting an increased basal coronary vasomotor tone. [11] Invasive physiology corroborates this: in functional angiography, CSFP was associated with low flow velocity and higher microvascular resistance at rest as compared with patients without CSFP. [12]

Endothelial dysfunction is a recurrent theme. Endothelin-1 and nitric oxide concentrations in slow coronary flow patients were assessed before and at the peak of exercise stress testing and compared with healthy controls, revealing impaired endothelial responses [13]. Systemic inflammation may also contribute, as plasma concentrations of CRP and IL-6 increased and were positively correlated with TIMI frame count in patients with SCF compared with normal coronary flow subjects. [14] Intracoronary studies further suggest that coronary microvascular spasm can be the underlying pathophysiological mechanism of the slow coronary flow phenomenon. [15] However, the relationship between CTFC and formal microvascular indices is imperfect; one study found that corrected TIMI frame count had weak negative correlation with basal average peak velocity and weak positive correlation with basal microvascular resistance. [6]

## Clinical Presentation and Prognosis

The dominant symptom is angina, often recurrent. The clinical implications are significant, with over 80% of patients experiencing recurrent chest pain, resulting in considerable impairment in quality of life. [2] CSFP can also mimic acute coronary syndromes and, rarely, provoke malignant arrhythmias. Clinically, it can present as angina pectoris, acute coronary syndrome and sudden cardiac death. [7] Repolarization abnormalities may underlie this risk; investigators evaluated the effects of slow coronary artery flow on QT interval duration and QT dispersion as a possible indicator of increased risk for ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. [16] Persistence of the angiographic abnormality on serial study is variable [17].

## Management

There is no firmly established therapy. Various medications have been evaluated for the treatment of CSFP. However, the actual efficacies of the majority of these pharmacological agents have not been established. [18] Calcium channel blockade is the best-studied approach: in a randomized crossover trial, without changing epicardial vessel diameter or rate-pressure product, mibefradil reduced the number of vessels exhibiting TIMI-2 flow from 18 to 5, and significantly improved the TIMI frame count in those vessels exhibiting TIMI-2 flow. [19] Intracoronary calcium channel blockers acutely normalize flow, and oral agents may provide durable relief; in one series, based on a positive intracoronary response to nifedipine, oral CCBs were subsequently started in all 15 patients with significant symptomatic improvement at follow-up. [18]

Agents targeting endothelial function have also been explored. Oral dipyridamole has been reported to improve angiographic flow [20], statins may improve perfusion through anti-inflammatory and endothelial effects [21,22], and nebivolol—a beta-blocker with nitric-oxide-mediated vasodilation—improved flow-mediated dilation, with chest pain relief detected in 38 patients after treatment (90%). [23] Nebivolol may additionally mitigate arrhythmic risk, as one study found that coronary slow flow is associated with increased QT dispersion, and nebivolol reduced increased QT dispersion in patients with CSF after three months. [24]

## Conclusion

CSFP is a recognizable, relatively common, and often symptomatic disorder of coronary microcirculatory function that should be actively sought rather than dismissed as an angiographic curiosity [25]. Its pathophysiology—blending microvascular structural change, endothelial dysfunction, raised vasomotor tone, microvascular spasm, and inflammation—remains incompletely defined [2,5,10,15]. The lack of large randomized therapeutic trials means management remains empirical, and standardized diagnostic criteria and adequately powered studies are needed to clarify its relationship to broader microvascular angina [6,18,26–30].
